new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent, to the extent it is perceptible at all, falls on the first syllable of the word; separately, at the end of a sentence the pitch rises and the penultimate syllable (of the sentence-final word) is stressed, i.e. a phrase-final penultimate prominence overlaid on weak word-initial accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the hedge 'where noticeable' signals that word accent is weak. No statement about long vowels attracting accent, though vowel length is described as distinctive (long vowels written double).
new_statements.domain_note: Two domains are distinguished in the one sentence: word-level accent (initial) versus sentence-final prosody (raised voice plus penultimate stress). Impressionistic missionary-era description based on five months at Fouia/Sulufou (Lau Lagoon, 'Lau proper') in 1927; no instrumental or metrical analysis. Consistent in direction with the left-edge (initial) stress described for the closely related North Malaitan language Toqabaqita in our catalog, but that is a different language and was not used as evidence here.
new_statements.identity_note: Ivens 1929 explicitly describes 'Lau proper' as spoken on Sulufou (Sulu Vou) and the other artificial islands of the Lau Lagoon, north-east coast of Malaita (fieldwork at Fouia, 1927) = Glottolog lauu1247. His earlier 1921 grammar (no stress statement) was based on the southern Lau of Port Adam (Ataa Cove emigrants), which he says is closer to the hill languages. Tryon 1995 distinguishes three Lau dialects (Suafa, Lau, Dai/Ndai); the statement pertains to the central Lau dialect.
